question:
Patient note:
A previously healthy 35-year-old man who works as a warehouse forklift operator was brought to the hospital’s critical care intake bay after collapsing at home with sudden epigastric pain and relentless vomiting that started eight hours earlier, shortly after he consumed a late-night meal heavy in fried foods and beer while celebrating a coworker’s promotion. According to his spouse, he awoke around 3 a.m. drenched in sweat, febrile to the touch, and retching non-bloody, non-bilious fluid every 15–20 minutes; shortly before sunrise he became visibly short of breath and increasingly restless, prompting an emergency call. Emergency medical technicians found him sitting upright on the bathroom floor, clutching his upper abdomen yet conversant and oriented; fingertip saturation on ambient air registered in the low 70s, so they applied a non-rebreather mask that the respiratory therapist later measured to be delivering 55 % inspired oxygen. No intravenous fluids, antiemetics, analgesics, antibiotics, or steroids were administered during the 12-minute transport, and he received no nebulized bronchodilators or vasopressors en route. On stretcher arrival to the resuscitation bay—prior to any hospital-initiated therapy—vital signs were recorded as oral temperature 102.4 °F (39.1 °C), heart rate 110 beats per minute with a regular rhythm, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute with moderate accessory-muscle use, and manual blood pressure 122/65 mm Hg confirmed by automated cuff. He opened his eyes spontaneously, answered orientation questions appropriately, and obeyed multi-step commands, yielding a Glasgow Coma Score of 15 in the absence of sedatives, intoxicants, or head trauma. Skin examination revealed flushed, hot, diaphoretic integument without cyanosis or petechiae; capillary refill was brisk and there was no peripheral edema. Inspection of the conjunctivae showed mild scleral injection but no icterus. Jugular venous pulsations were not distended at 30 degrees. Cardiac auscultation disclosed a crisp S1, physiologic split S2, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops. Breath sounds were diminished bilaterally at the bases with diffuse fine crackles but no wheezes; percussion was dull posteriorly. The abdomen was distended, tympanitic, and exquisitely tender in the epigastrium and left upper quadrant without peritoneal rebound; bowel sounds were hypoactive. There was no flank bruising or Cullen sign. Neurologic screening found symmetric strength, intact sensation, and equal, briskly reactive pupils. A radial arterial sample drawn within 10 minutes of bay entry while he remained on 55 % oxygen revealed pH 7.36, PaCO₂ 34 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 60 mm Hg, corresponding to an alarming alveolar–arterial gradient of 537 mm Hg flagged as critical by the blood-gas analyzer. Simultaneously obtained chemistry showed serum sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 102 mmol/L, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L, glucose 124 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen 14 mg/dL, and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, consistent with preserved renal function despite ongoing emesis. Complete blood count demonstrated white blood cell count 18 000 cells/mm³ with 82 % neutrophils, hematocrit 40 %, hemoglobin 13.8 g/dL, and platelets 246 000/µL. Serum lipase drawn on arrival returned markedly elevated at 2 362 U/L, and lactate measured 2.1 mmol/L. A portable anteroposterior chest radiograph acquired before any intravenous fluid or antibiotic therapy showed low lung volumes, bibasilar patchy opacities, and a small left pleural effusion without free subdiaphragmatic air. Focused bedside ultrasound demonstrated an edematous, hypoechoic pancreas with peripancreatic fluid, a contracted gallbladder devoid of stones, a small, vigorously contracting left ventricle, and a collapsible inferior vena cava measuring 1.3 cm. Electrocardiography performed 15 minutes after arrival revealed sinus tachycardia at 108 beats per minute without ischemic changes or conduction delays. Urinalysis from a clean-catch specimen showed 1+ ketones but no bilirubin or hematuria; urinary output was 90 mL of concentrated yellow urine in the first 45 minutes of observation before catheter placement. Blood cultures, serum triglycerides, and a comprehensive hepatic panel were sent but results were pending at the moment the intensive care team agreed to accept the patient for aggressive fluid resuscitation, pain control, empiric antimicrobial coverage for possible infected necrosis, and close monitoring of respiratory mechanics given the profound gas-exchange abnormality. Importantly, during the approximately 40 minutes between stretcher entry and ICU handoff he received neither crystalloids, opioids, antiemetics, antipyretics, antibiotics, corticosteroids, nor vasopressors, ensuring that the documented temperature of 102.4 °F, pulse 110 beats per minute, respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute, blood pressure 122/65 mm Hg, arterial pH 7.36, serum sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, hematocrit 40 %, white blood cell count 18 000/mm³, inspired oxygen fraction 55 %, and alveolar–arterial gradient 537 mm Hg accurately reflect his untreated physiological state at the time of intensive care admission for suspected severe acute pancreatitis complicated by early acute lung injury.

Question: What is the patient's APACHE II score?
solution:
APACHE II adds acute physiology, age, and chronic health points. Using the supplied admission measurements:
• Temperature 39.1 °C (39–40.9): 3. Mean arterial pressure = (122 + 2×65)/3 = 84 mm Hg (70–109): 0.
• Heart rate 110/min (110–139): 2. Respiratory rate 26/min (25–34): 1.
• FiO₂ is 0.55, so use the A–a gradient rather than PaO₂. The reported gradient of 537 mm Hg (≥500) scores 4.
• Arterial pH 7.36: 0. Sodium 136 mmol/L: 0. Potassium 4.0 mmol/L: 0. Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL: 0.
• Hematocrit 40%: 0. WBC 18,000/mm³ (15,000–39,999): 1. Neurologic points = 15 − GCS 15 = 0.
• Age 35 (<45): 0. No severe chronic organ insufficiency or immunocompromise: 0.
Total = (3 + 0 + 2 + 1 + 4 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 1 + 0) + 0 + 0 = 11.
Final answer: 11
